title: What is the Spark Web UI (`localhost:4040` during a running app, History Server for completed apps), what tabs do you use for debugging — Jobs (overall progress), Stages (task duration spread, shuffle read/write, GC time), SQL (query plan, AQE decisions), Storage (cached data), Executors (memory, cores, failed tasks) — and what patterns indicate problems (one task 10x slower = skew, high GC time = memory pressure, large shuffle write = expensive wide transformation)?
shortTitle: The Spark Web UI and debugging with it

s1_definition.profdef: The Spark Web UI is the built-in monitoring interface for a Spark application, served at port 4040 on the driver while an application is running and preserved for completed applications by the Spark History Server. It presents the application's execution through several tabs: Jobs shows overall progress and the job-to-stage breakdown, Stages shows per-task metrics including duration spread, shuffle read and write, and garbage-collection time, SQL shows the query plan and Adaptive Query Execution decisions for DataFrame and SQL queries, Storage shows cached and persisted data, and Executors shows per-executor memory, cores, task counts, and failures. You debug by reading characteristic patterns: one task taking many times longer than its peers indicates data skew, a high fraction of time in garbage collection indicates memory pressure, and a large shuffle write indicates an expensive wide transformation.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India the Spark Web UI is like the live operations dashboard in the branch manager's office, and the History Server is the archive of past days' dashboards. Each tab is a different view: Jobs is the overall "how far along is today's batch" board, Stages is the per-clerk breakdown showing who is slow and how much paperwork each is shuffling, SQL is the printed plan of how a complex report was executed, Storage shows which ledgers are kept handy on the shelf, and Executors shows each clerk's desk size, how many tasks they did, and whether any failed. You diagnose trouble by spotting tell-tale patterns — one clerk taking ten times longer means they got an unfair pile (skew), clerks spending their day tidying their desks means desks are too small (memory pressure), and mountains of paper being shuffled between desks means an expensive reorganization step.
s1_definition.oneliner: The Spark UI (port 4040 live, History Server for completed apps) debugs through Jobs, Stages, SQL, Storage, and Executors tabs — one task far slower means skew, high GC time means memory pressure, and large shuffle write means an expensive wide transformation.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** The Spark Web UI is the built-in monitoring interface for a Spark application, served at port 4040 on the driver while an application is running and preserved for completed applications by the Spark History Server. It presents the application's execution through several tabs: Jobs shows overall progress and the job-to-stage breakdown, Stages shows per-task metrics including duration spread, shuffle read and write, and garbage-collection time, SQL shows the query plan and Adaptive Query Execution decisions for DataFrame and SQL queries, Storage shows cached and persisted data, and Executors shows per-executor memory, cores, task counts, and failures. You debug by reading characteristic patterns: one task taking many times longer than its peers indicates data skew, a high fraction of time in garbage collection indicates memory pressure, and a large shuffle write indicates an expensive wide transformation.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India the Spark Web UI is like the live operations dashboard in the branch manager's office, and the History Server is the archive of past days' dashboards. Each tab is a different view: Jobs is the overall "how far along is today's batch" board, Stages is the per-clerk breakdown showing who is slow and how much paperwork each is shuffling, SQL is the printed plan of how a complex report was executed, Storage shows which ledgers are kept handy on the shelf, and Executors shows each clerk's desk size, how many tasks they did, and whether any failed. You diagnose trouble by spotting tell-tale patterns — one clerk taking ten times longer means they got an unfair pile (skew), clerks spending their day tidying their desks means desks are too small (memory pressure), and mountains of paper being shuffled between desks means an expensive reorganization step.

**One line to remember:** The Spark UI (port 4040 live, History Server for completed apps) debugs through Jobs, Stages, SQL, Storage, and Executors tabs — one task far slower means skew, high GC time means memory pressure, and large shuffle write means an expensive wide transformation.

sections.s2_technical:
The UI is served by the driver at port 4040 while the application runs, incrementing the port if one is taken, and it disappears when the application ends. To inspect completed applications you use the Spark History Server, which reads event logs that Spark writes when spark.eventLog.enabled is on, and renders the same tabs after the fact. In production you rely on the History Server because live jobs finish and you need to investigate afterward.

The Jobs tab gives the top-level view: each action triggers a job, and the tab shows each job's status, duration, and the stages it comprises, with a timeline. You start here to see which job is slow or failed and then drill into its stages. The Stages tab is the workhorse for performance debugging, because it shows per-task metrics within a stage: the distribution of task durations, the input and shuffle read and write sizes per task, and the time spent in garbage collection. The event timeline and the summary quantiles — minimum, median, and maximum — are where skew and imbalance become visible.

The SQL tab applies to DataFrame and Spark SQL queries and shows the query plan as a graph of operators with their row counts and timings, including whether a join was a broadcast or sort-merge join and what Adaptive Query Execution decided at runtime, such as coalescing partitions or switching a join strategy. This is where you confirm that predicate pushdown and broadcast happened as expected. The Storage tab shows cached and persisted datasets, how many partitions are cached, and how much memory and disk they occupy, which is how you check whether caching is effective or whether over-caching is squeezing execution memory. The Executors tab shows each executor's memory usage, core count, active and completed and failed task counts, shuffle totals, and garbage-collection time, which is how you spot an executor under memory pressure or losing tasks.

Reading patterns is the actual skill. In the Stages tab, if the maximum task duration and maximum shuffle read are many times the median while most tasks finished quickly, one partition is far larger than the rest — data skew — and the fix is AQE skew join, salting, or isolate-and-broadcast. In the Executors tab, if garbage-collection time is a large fraction of task time, the executors are thrashing near their memory limit — memory pressure — often from over-caching or too few partitions, visible together with spill in the Stages tab. A large shuffle write on a stage signals an expensive wide transformation like a big join or groupBy, prompting you to reduce shuffle volume by pre-aggregating or pruning, or to tune partition counts. A senior-level nuance is correlating tabs rather than reading one in isolation: a slow job in Jobs leads to a specific stage in Stages, whose task distribution reveals skew, which you corroborate with the Executors GC time and the SQL plan to decide whether the cause is skew, memory, an unexpected join strategy, or a missing broadcast. You also enable event logging so the History Server captures everything, because the most important debugging often happens after the job has finished and the live UI is gone.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — A National Bank of India nightly job is slow. The engineer starts in Jobs, finds the slow stage, and in Stages sees one task with ten times the median duration and shuffle read — data skew on a pooling account.

Problem 2 — Another job's Executors tab shows garbage-collection time at forty percent of task time — memory pressure, confirmed by heavy spill in Stages and a large cache in Storage.

Problem 3 — A third job's Stages tab shows a huge shuffle write on one stage — an expensive wide transformation that should be pre-aggregated or have more partitions.

The demo models a UI-metrics analyzer that, given a stage's task quantiles, executor GC fraction, and shuffle write size, reports the diagnosis an engineer would read from the Web UI, logging the pattern and the recommended action.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: four stage-metric snapshots an engineer would read from the Web UI — a join stage with one task forty times the median, an aggregation stage with forty percent garbage-collection time, a groupBy stage with eighty gigabytes of shuffle write, and a healthy filter stage.

Step 1: The join stage is analyzed. Its maximum task time of forty thousand milliseconds is forty times the median of one thousand, above the ten-times skew threshold, so the reader diagnoses data skew and recommends the skew toolkit.

Step 2: The aggregation stage is analyzed. Its garbage-collection fraction of forty percent exceeds the high-GC threshold, so the reader diagnoses memory pressure and recommends reducing caching and adding partitions or memory.

Step 3: The groupBy stage is analyzed. Its shuffle write of eighty thousand megabytes exceeds the large-shuffle threshold, so the reader diagnoses an expensive wide transformation and recommends pre-aggregating or pruning before the shuffle and tuning partitions.

Step 4: The filter stage is analyzed. Its task times are even, its garbage collection is low, and its shuffle write is tiny, so the reader reports it as healthy with no problem pattern. The demo logs each stage's diagnosis, reproducing how an engineer reads the UI tabs to classify each stage.

Final output:

```

2026-10-30 06:09:00 WARNING agg-stage: GC 40% of task time → MEMORY PRESSURE

2026-10-30 06:09:00 WARNING groupby-stage: shuffle write 80000MB → EXPENSIVE WIDE TRANSFORMATION
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Spark Web UI is the built-in monitoring interface, served by the driver at port 4040 while an application runs and preserved for completed applications by the History Server, which reads the event logs Spark writes when event logging is enabled. In production I rely on the History Server, because live jobs finish and the most important debugging usually happens afterward. I navigate through its tabs: Jobs for overall progress and to find which job is slow or failed, Stages for per-task metrics like the duration spread, shuffle read and write, and garbage-collection time, SQL for the query plan and the Adaptive Query Execution decisions such as broadcast switches and partition coalescing, Storage for cached data, and Executors for per-executor memory, cores, task counts, and failures.

The real skill is reading the characteristic patterns. In the Stages tab, when the maximum task duration and shuffle read are many times the median while most tasks finish quickly, one partition is far larger than the rest, which is data skew, and I fix it with AQE skew join, salting, or isolate-and-broadcast. In the Executors tab, when garbage-collection time is a large fraction of task time, the executors are thrashing near their memory limit, which is memory pressure, usually from over-caching or too few partitions and corroborated by spill in the Stages tab and cache size in the Storage tab. A large shuffle write on a stage signals an expensive wide transformation like a big join or groupBy, prompting me to pre-aggregate or prune before the shuffle or tune partition counts.

At the National Bank of India this was my standard triage. A slow nightly job led me from the Jobs tab to a specific stage, whose task distribution in the Stages tab showed one task with ten times the median duration — skew on a pooling account — which I confirmed against the Executors GC time and the SQL plan before applying the skew fix. I always correlate tabs rather than read one in isolation, because a slow job, a skewed stage, high GC, and an unexpected join strategy together tell a coherent story, and I always enable event logging so the History Server captures everything for after-the-fact investigation. The one-line summary I give in interviews is: Jobs to localize, Stages for task skew and shuffle, Executors for GC and failures, SQL for the plan and AQE, Storage for caching — and the three signatures to memorize are one task far slower means skew, high GC means memory pressure, and a large shuffle write means an expensive wide transformation.
